variants.title: Write a reproducible rubric
variants.context: A rubric is an evaluation contract. Name the decision it serves, anchor each label in observable evidence, calibrate against an independently reviewed set by slice, then predeclare the escalation limits before any release candidate is evaluated.
variants.prompt: A rubric currently says to score answers as excellent, adequate, or poor based on how helpful they feel. Put the repair steps in order.

items.text: Run the anchored rubric against an independently reviewed set, reporting agreement by language and risk tier.
State that this rubric routes support answers to human review and does not by itself block a release.
Set the agreement, bias, and critical-miss limits and name the human owner who receives failed slices.
Replace each adjective with the observable evidence that earns the label, and add near-boundary examples.

variants.hint: Decide what the result is for before deciding what the labels mean.
variants.explanation: One judge prompt should not silently serve ranking, regression detection, routing, and release blocking at once.

variants.title: Write a reproducible rubric
variants.context: A rubric is an evaluation contract. Name the decision it serves, anchor each label in observable evidence, calibrate against an independently reviewed set by slice, then predeclare the escalation limits before any release candidate is evaluated.
variants.prompt: One judge prompt is being used to rank models, catch regressions, route review, and block releases. Put the steps that untangle it in order.

items.text: Declare the coverage and agreement floors and the escalation path before the next release candidate is scored.
Define the evidence that earns each label for that decision, separating dimensions that can fail independently.
Compare the rubric against independently reviewed cases across domains and response lengths, keeping panel disagreement.
Pick the single decision this prompt will serve and move the other three to their own rubrics.

variants.hint: A rubric that serves four decisions is calibrated for none of them.
variants.explanation: Scope first, then anchors, then calibration evidence, then policy. Reordering these hides uncertainty as false precision.

variants.title: Write a reproducible rubric
variants.context: A rubric is an evaluation contract. Name the decision it serves, anchor each label in observable evidence, calibrate against an independently reviewed set by slice, then predeclare the escalation limits before any release candidate is evaluated.
variants.prompt: An anchored rubric was calibrated only on English cases and the product is launching in three more languages. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Add boundary examples in each new language so the labels do not depend on translation quality alone.
Set a per-language agreement floor and route any language below it to the named reviewer.
Confirm the rubric still serves one decision, which is blocking a release on grounded-answer quality.
Score an independently reviewed set per language and report matches and totals for each one.

variants.hint: Which step turns a per-language weakness into something the gate can act on?
variants.explanation: Calibration is measured by slice. An aggregate agreement number can stay healthy while one language falls below its floor.

variants.title: Aggregate both orders
variants.context: Pairwise judging runs both candidate orders. Each raw judgment is translated from position back to candidate identity, and a preference is reported only when the two orders agree. Disagreement becomes an abstention that a human reviews.
variants.prompt: A pairwise item has been judged as A then B, and again as B then A. Put the aggregation steps in order.

items.text: Report the shared preference when they agree, or abstain and flag human review when they do not.
Check that the second judgment reverses the same candidate pair and uses the same rubric and judge versions.
Compare the two identity-mapped preferences to see whether swapping the order changed the winner.
Translate each raw judgment from the position it names to the candidate identity that won.

variants.hint: Position labels mean nothing until they are mapped back to candidate identity.
variants.explanation: A preference is reported only when both orders agree by identity. Otherwise the judge abstains instead of inventing a winner.

variants.title: Aggregate both orders
variants.context: Pairwise judging runs both candidate orders. Each raw judgment is translated from position back to candidate identity, and a preference is reported only when the two orders agree. Disagreement becomes an abstention that a human reviews.
variants.prompt: In the first order the judge preferred the second position, and in the reversed order it preferred the first position. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Map the reversed order's first-position winner back to candidate B as well.
Verify both judgments cover the same reversed pair under one rubric version and one judge version.
Report candidate B, because both orders agree once positions are resolved to identities.
Map the first order's second-position winner back to candidate B.

variants.hint: Different positions can name the same candidate.
variants.explanation: Order consistency is checked after mapping to identity, so a stable preference survives the swap.

variants.title: Aggregate both orders
variants.context: Pairwise judging runs both candidate orders. Each raw judgment is translated from position back to candidate identity, and a preference is reported only when the two orders agree. Disagreement becomes an abstention that a human reviews.
variants.prompt: The first order returned abstain and the reversed order picked the first position. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Route the item to human review rather than adopting the answer from the order that decided.
Carry the first order's abstention through unchanged, because an abstention has no position to resolve.
Map the reversed order's first-position winner back to candidate A.
Verify the two judgments reverse the same pair and share the rubric and judge versions.
Record that the two orders disagree, so the item cannot report a winner.

variants.hint: One decided order does not outrank a disagreement.
variants.explanation: Disagreement between orders becomes an abstention with human review, which keeps uncertainty visible in the result.

variants.title: Compute the gate rate
variants.context: Gates read counts with their denominators, not bare percentages. A gate rate is the numerator divided by its declared denominator, multiplied by one hundred.
variants.prompt: A controlled position-bias probe judges 60 pairs in both orders. The judge names a different winner in 9 of those pairs. What is the order-flip rate in percent?
variants.hint: The denominator is the thing the probe counts, not the number of model calls it made.
variants.explanation: An order-flip rate is flipped pairs divided by probed pairs. Each pair is judged twice, but it is still one pair.

mistakes.feedback: You divided by 120 judgments; the probe counts pairs, and each pair was judged twice.
That is the flip count, not a rate.

variants.title: Compute the gate rate
variants.context: Gates read counts with their denominators, not bare percentages. A gate rate is the numerator divided by its declared denominator, multiplied by one hundred.
variants.prompt: A critical language slice has 60 decided cases, and the judge matches the human panel on 51 of them. The declared slice floor is 90 percent. What is the measured slice agreement in percent?
variants.hint: The gate is written on agreement, so build the numerator from matches.
variants.explanation: Slice agreement is panel matches divided by decided cases in that slice. Reporting it beside the aggregate is what makes the floor enforceable.

mistakes.feedback: That is the disagreement rate; this gate reads agreement.
That is the count of disagreements, not a rate.

variants.title: Compute the gate rate
variants.context: Gates read counts with their denominators, not bare percentages. A gate rate is the numerator divided by its declared denominator, multiplied by one hundred.
variants.prompt: A stability probe sends the same 140 items through the judge twice. The two runs return different labels on 7 items. What is the repeat-disagreement rate in percent?
variants.hint: Read which direction the limit is written in before choosing the numerator.
variants.explanation: Repeat disagreement is unstable items divided by repeated items. The limit is a maximum, so the numerator counts failures.

mistakes.feedback: That is the repeat agreement rate; this limit is written on disagreement.
You divided by 280 judgments; the probe repeats 140 items.

variants.title: Decide what the judge may claim
variants.context: A judge is useful when the criterion is observable in the supplied evidence and an occasional disagreement is bounded. It should be able to return abstain or needs review, and it must not become the unnamed owner of a consequential decision.
variants.prompt: A team needs to check that support answers carry the required sections and stay inside a length limit, across 8,000 responses per week.
options: Send every response to trained human reviewers before release.
Let a judge apply the anchored rubric and sample its disagreements for review.
Drop the check, because a judge result is not ground truth.
optionFeedback: Full human review is not affordable here and the criterion is plainly observable in the output.
The criterion is visible in the supplied evidence and a rare disagreement is cheap, which is the good case for a judge.
A judge result is evidence about a declared rubric, and that is enough for a bounded formatting decision.
variants.hint: Ask whether the criterion is observable and what one disagreement actually costs.
variants.explanation: Format compliance is a good judge candidate because the evidence is present and the consequence of a miss is bounded.

variants.title: Decide what the judge may claim
variants.context: A judge is useful when the criterion is observable in the supplied evidence and an occasional disagreement is bounded. It should be able to return abstain or needs review, and it must not become the unnamed owner of a consequential decision.
variants.prompt: A lender wants the judge to approve or reject final credit-decision letters, with no named human owner for the outcome.
options: Use a stronger judge model with a longer and more detailed rubric.
Keep approval with qualified humans and let the judge surface evidence and disagreements.
Raise the calibration sample until the agreement interval is narrow enough.
optionFeedback: A stronger judge changes the quality of the evidence, not who is accountable for the decision.
Irreversible, high-impact approvals need a qualified human owner; the judge organizes evidence for that owner.
A narrower interval measures the rubric better and still leaves a consequential decision unowned.
variants.hint: Ask who is accountable when this decision is wrong.
variants.explanation: Appeals, legal and financial approvals, and irreversible actions are poor judge candidates regardless of measured agreement.

variants.title: Decide what the judge may claim
variants.context: A judge is useful when the criterion is observable in the supplied evidence and an occasional disagreement is bounded. It should be able to return abstain or needs review, and it must not become the unnamed owner of a consequential decision.
variants.prompt: On roughly one case in twelve the supplied evidence does not let the rubric separate two labels. The team wants full label coverage.
options: Let the judge return needs review and route those cases to the owner.
Average the two candidate labels into a middle score.
Force the nearer label so every case carries a score.
optionFeedback: Abstention keeps the uncertainty visible and sends the undecidable cases to the person who can resolve them.
A midpoint invents a value that no rubric label actually supports.
Forcing a label converts missing evidence into false precision that the gate cannot see.
variants.hint: What should happen when the rubric genuinely cannot decide?
variants.explanation: Forcing a score when the rubric is ambiguous hides uncertainty. Abstention plus routing preserves it as evidence.

variants.title: Name the judge failure
variants.context: One overall agreement number can hide several different failures. Position bias, verbosity bias, self-inconsistency, slice failure, panel mismatch, and judge leakage are probed separately because passing one probe says nothing about the others.
variants.prompt: A calibration report lists four symptoms. Match each symptom to the failure it indicates.

pairs.label: Position bias
pairs.detail: The preferred candidate changes when the pair is shown as B then A.

pairs.label: Verbosity bias
pairs.detail: The longer and more polished answer wins even when controlled evidence favors the concise one.

pairs.label: Self-inconsistency
pairs.detail: Repeated judgments of the same item return different labels beyond the allowed rate.

pairs.label: Slice failure
pairs.detail: Aggregate agreement looks healthy while one language sits below its floor.

variants.hint: Ask what was held constant and what was varied in each observation.
variants.explanation: Each failure has its own probe. A low order-flip rate does not prove the absence of verbosity bias.

variants.title: Name the judge failure
variants.context: One overall agreement number can hide several different failures. Position bias, verbosity bias, self-inconsistency, slice failure, panel mismatch, and judge leakage are probed separately because passing one probe says nothing about the others.
variants.prompt: A team is designing controlled probes. Match each probe design to the failure it is built to expose.

pairs.label: Order-swap probe
pairs.detail: Judge every pair twice with the candidates in both positions.

pairs.label: Style-controlled pairs
pairs.detail: Hold the content constant and vary only length and polish.

pairs.label: Repeat runs
pairs.detail: Send the identical item through the same judge more than once.

pairs.label: Per-slice denominators
pairs.detail: Report matches and totals separately for each language and risk tier.

variants.hint: Match the variable the probe moves to the bias that variable would trigger.
variants.explanation: Probes are run separately because each one holds a different thing constant. Repeated agreement is not correctness.

variants.title: Name the judge failure
variants.context: One overall agreement number can hide several different failures. Position bias, verbosity bias, self-inconsistency, slice failure, panel mismatch, and judge leakage are probed separately because passing one probe says nothing about the others.
variants.prompt: Four observations arrive from one release batch. Match each observation to the failure it indicates.

pairs.label: Judge leakage
pairs.detail: The evaluator consistently prefers answers written by its own model family.

pairs.label: Panel mismatch
pairs.detail: The judge confidently disagrees with qualified reviewers on the highest-impact cases.

pairs.label: Position bias
pairs.detail: Twelve of eighty pairs reverse their winner when the order is swapped.

pairs.label: Slice failure
pairs.detail: Overall agreement is 92 percent while the billing cohort sits at 61 percent.

variants.hint: Two of these are visible only when results are split by candidate family or cohort.
variants.explanation: Averaging disagreement away hides which of these failures is present, so each is reported with its own numerator and denominator.
